questions.question_text: A projectile is fired from the origin at $34\text{ m/s}$ at $30^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$. Integrating $\ddot{y}=-10$ gives $\dot{y}=-10t+C$. What is $C$?

options.why: Used the horizontal component $34\cos 30^{\circ}$ instead of the vertical component.
Made the initial upward velocity negative, confusing it with the sign of the acceleration.
Both slips: cosine used instead of sine and the initial velocity given the wrong sign.

questions.question_text: A ball is thrown from the origin at $12\text{ m/s}$ at $60^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$. Which is $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$?

options.why: Applied gravity to the horizontal component as well, but $\ddot{x}=0$.
Swapped sine and cosine when resolving the initial speed.
Both slips: components swapped and gravity applied to the horizontal component.

questions.question_text: A projectile launched from the origin has $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)=7\underset{\sim}{i}+(26-9.8t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres per second. Which is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$?

options.why: Integrated $-9.8t$ as $-9.8t^{2}$, forgetting to halve the coefficient.
Left the constant horizontal velocity un-integrated, so $x$ does not grow with time.
Both slips: the horizontal term not integrated and the $t^{2}$ coefficient not halved.

questions.question_text: A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff $16\text{ m}$ above the sea, with $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)=13\underset{\sim}{i}+(22-10t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres per second and $y$ measured from sea level. Which is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$?

options.why: Assumed launch from ground level, dropping the $16\text{ m}$ height of the cliff.
Put the launch height into the horizontal component instead of the vertical one.
Added the launch height to both components, although the stone starts at $x=0$.

questions.question_text:
A projectile leaves the origin at $V\text{ m/s}$ at angle $\alpha$ above the horizontal, with $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$. A student writes:
Line 1: $\underset{\sim}{\ddot{r}}=-10\underset{\sim}{j}$
Line 2: $\underset{\sim}{v}=C_{1}\underset{\sim}{i}+(-10t+C_{2})\underset{\sim}{j}$
Line 3: $C_{1}=V\sin\alpha$ and $C_{2}=V\cos\alpha$
Line 4: $\underset{\sim}{r}=Vt\sin\alpha\,\underset{\sim}{i}+(-5t^{2}+Vt\cos\alpha)\underset{\sim}{j}$
Which is the first incorrect line?

options.why: Expects gravity to appear in the $\underset{\sim}{i}$ component too, but there is no horizontal force.
Expects integrating $0$ to give $0$, rather than the arbitrary constant $C_{1}$.
Spots the swapped components only where they are carried forward, not where they first appear.

questions.solution_text:
Lines 1 and 2 are correct.
At $t=0$ the horizontal component is $V\cos\alpha$ and the vertical component is $V\sin\alpha$, so Line 3 has them the wrong way round.
Line 3 is the first incorrect line.

questions.question_text: A particle is projected from the origin at $10\text{ m/s}$ at $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$ above the horizontal. Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$. Which pair gives $x$ and $y$?

options.why: Swapped sine and cosine when resolving the initial speed.
Integrated $-10t$ as $-10t^{2}$ instead of $-5t^{2}$.
Both slips: components swapped and the $t^{2}$ coefficient not halved.

questions.question_text: A ball is thrown from the origin at $20\text{ m/s}$ at $30^{\circ}$ **below** the horizontal. Take $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^{2}$. Which is $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$?

options.why: Treated the launch as above the horizontal, giving a positive initial vertical velocity.
Swapped sine and cosine when resolving the initial speed.
Both slips: components swapped and the downward launch treated as upward.

questions.question_text: A ball launched from a platform has $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=21t\underset{\sim}{i}+(28t-4.9t^{2}+5)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres, with $y$ measured from the ground. What value of $g$ was used, and what are the launch height and the launch speed?

options.why: Read $g$ straight off the $t^{2}$ coefficient without doubling it.
Added the component sizes $21+28$ instead of using Pythagoras for the speed.
Both slips: $g$ not doubled and the speed found by adding the components.

questions.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)=21\underset{\sim}{i}+(28-9.8t)\underset{\sim}{j}$
$\underset{\sim}{\ddot{r}}=-9.8\underset{\sim}{j}$, so $g=9.8$
$\underset{\sim}{r}(0)=5\underset{\sim}{j}$, so the launch height is $5\text{ m}$.
$V=\sqrt{21^{2}+28^{2}}$
$=\sqrt{1225}$
$=35$
